questions.stem:
Statements: A > B ≥ C = D < E
Conclusions:
I. A > C
II. B ≥ D

options.option_text: Only conclusion I definitively follows
Both conclusion I and II definitively follow
Only conclusion II definitively follows
Neither conclusion I nor II definitively follow

questions.explanation: From the statements, A > B and B ≥ C. Combining these, A > C (Conclusion I follows). Also, since B ≥ C and C = D, substituting D for C gives B ≥ D (Conclusion II follows). Therefore, both conclusions are logically true.

questions.stem:
Statements: P < Q ≤ R = S > T
Conclusions:
I. P < S
II. R > T

options.option_text: Only conclusion I definitively follows
Only conclusion II definitively follows
Both conclusion I and II definitively follow
Neither conclusion I nor II definitively follow

questions.explanation: From the statements, P < Q ≤ R = S. Comparing P and S across the chain gives P < S (Conclusion I follows). Also, since R = S and S > T, substituting R for S gives R > T (Conclusion II follows). Both are true.

questions.stem:
Statements: M ≥ N > O = P ≤ Q
Conclusions:
I. M > P
II. N > Q

options.option_text: Only conclusion II definitively follows
Both conclusion I and II definitively follow
Neither conclusion I nor II definitively follow
Only conclusion I definitively follows

questions.explanation: For I: M ≥ N > O = P. Tracing M to P involves a strict '>' sign, making M > P true. For II: N > O = P ≤ Q. Between N and Q, the signs face opposite directions (>, ≤), establishing no definite relationship. So II does not follow.

questions.stem:
Statements: W = X ≤ Y > Z; X ≥ U
Conclusions:
I. Y ≥ U
II. W > Z

options.option_text: Only conclusion I definitively follows
Only conclusion II definitively follows
Both conclusion I and II definitively follow
Neither conclusion I nor II definitively follow

questions.explanation: From the statements, U ≤ X ≤ Y. Combining these gives U ≤ Y or Y ≥ U (Conclusion I follows). For II, trace W to Z: W = X ≤ Y > Z. The signs face opposite directions (≤, >) between W and Z, meaning no definite relationship exists. Conclusion II does not follow.

questions.stem:
Statements: E < F = G ≥ H; G < I
Conclusions:
I. I > H
II. E < G

options.option_text: Only conclusion I definitively follows
Only conclusion II definitively follows
Both conclusion I and II definitively follow
Neither conclusion I nor II definitively follow

questions.explanation: For I: G ≥ H and I > G. Combining gives I > G ≥ H, so I > H (Conclusion I follows). For II: E < F and F = G. Substituting G for F gives E < G (Conclusion II follows). Both are completely true.

questions.stem:
In a coded language:
A @ B means A ≥ B
A # B means A > B
A $ B means A = B
A * B means A ≤ B
A % B means A < B
Statements: P @ Q, Q $ R, R # S
Conclusions: I. P # S  II. P @ R

options.option_text: Only conclusion I definitively follows
Both conclusion I and II definitively follow
Only conclusion II definitively follows
Neither conclusion I nor II definitively follow

questions.explanation: Decoding the statements gives: P ≥ Q, Q = R, R > S. Combined: P ≥ Q = R > S. For Conclusion I: P # S means P > S. Tracing P to S shows P > S is indeed true. For Conclusion II: P @ R means P ≥ R. Since P ≥ Q and Q = R, P ≥ R is also true. Both follow.

questions.stem:
Using the same code as above:
Statements: M * N, N % O, O $ P, P @ Q
Conclusions: I. M % P  II. N % Q

options.option_text: Only conclusion II definitively follows
Both conclusion I and II definitively follow
Neither conclusion I nor II definitively follow
Only conclusion I definitively follows

questions.explanation: Decoding gives: M ≤ N, N < O, O = P, P ≥ Q. Combined: M ≤ N < O = P ≥ Q. For Conclusion I: M % P means M < P. Tracing M to P shows M < P is true. For Conclusion II: N % Q means N < Q. Tracing N to Q shows N < O = P ≥ Q. The opposite signs (<, ≥) mean no definite relation exists between N and Q. So II does not follow.
